The journalist therefore made the correction easy to understand and included links to the official transport service. Residents began sharing the verified information, and the journalist reflected on how quickly rumors could spread during emergencies.

questions.prompt: If you were the journalist after seeing the viral post, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would feel pressure to respond quickly, but verifying the claim would remain more important than being first.

questions.prompt: Should social media companies remove false information during emergencies?
modelAnswers: They should respond promptly to demonstrably false claims that create safety risks, while providing transparent reasons and appeal procedures.

questions.prompt: Are people becoming less able to judge the reliability of information?
modelAnswers: Not necessarily, but the speed and volume of online content make careful verification increasingly important.

questions.prompt: Should schools teach students how to verify online information?
modelAnswers: Absolutely. Students should learn to compare sources, identify evidence, and recognize misleading images.

title: Tourism and Housing Prices
storyLeadIn: A mayor was hearing complaints from residents of a popular historic town.

panels.description: Tourists roll suitcases past homes being used as short-term rentals
Residents tell mayor that long-term housing has become expensive
Town introduces registration rules for short-term accommodation
Some homes return to long-term rental market and mayor reviews tourism impact

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A mayor was hearing complaints from residents of a popular historic town. Tourism had created local jobs, but more homes were becoming short-term rentals. However, residents increasingly complained that apartments were being turned into short-term tourist rentals, making homes harder to afford. The mayor organized a public consultation with landlords, residents, and hotel owners. After reviewing the information, the town introduced registration rules and limits in certain neighborhoods. Some apartments returned to the long-term rental market, but tourism businesses worried about fewer visitors. Some landlords feared that the new rules would reduce their income, while families hoped housing would become more affordable. The mayor asked officials to review the effects rather than judging the policy immediately. The mayor decided to monitor both housing costs and economic effects before making further changes.

questions.prompt: If you were the mayor facing these competing demands, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would look for a fair balance between tourism income and residents' ability to find affordable housing.

questions.prompt: Should cities limit the number of short-term holiday rentals?
modelAnswers: Limits can be justified where housing is scarce, but rules should reflect local conditions and be evaluated regularly.

questions.prompt: Do tourists have responsibilities toward residents of the places they visit?
modelAnswers: Yes. Visitors should respect local rules, reduce noise, and support businesses without damaging everyday community life.

questions.prompt: Should economic growth always be a government's main priority?
modelAnswers: No. Economic growth matters, but housing, social well-being, and environmental quality are also essential.

title: Lifelong Education for Workers
storyLeadIn: A training-center director was planning courses for adults whose jobs were changing.

panels.description: Factory workers learn that new machines will replace some tasks
Director meets local employers to identify needed skills
Training center offers evening courses in digital equipment
Workers complete courses and transfer to new positions

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A training-center director was planning courses for adults whose jobs were changing. Several local factories were planning to introduce new machines. Workers were anxious because they did not know whether their jobs would change or disappear. The director met with employers and identified skills that would be useful in the new workplaces. She organized affordable evening classes in digital equipment and basic data handling. Some workers were initially nervous about returning to study, but instructors offered individual support. The instructors divided participants into small groups according to their experience. Workers practiced realistic tasks using training equipment, and the center offered extra lessons for those who needed more time. After completing the courses, several participants moved into new roles, demonstrating that career development does not have to end after graduation.

questions.prompt: If you were the director speaking to worried workers, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would want to offer realistic opportunities without promising that every job could be protected.

questions.prompt: Should employers pay for workers to learn new skills?
modelAnswers: They should contribute, particularly when technological changes benefit the business and require employees to adapt.

questions.prompt: Will university degrees become less important in the future?
modelAnswers: Degrees will remain valuable, but short courses and practical experience may play a larger role throughout working life.

questions.prompt: Should governments support adults who return to education?
modelAnswers: Yes. Financial aid and flexible schedules can help people adapt to changes in the labor market.

title: Choosing a Community Energy Site
storyLeadIn: A regional council was considering where to build a new renewable-energy facility.

panels.description: Council displays map showing possible solar farm near farmland
Farmers and environmentalists express different concerns at meeting
Council orders independent studies and moves facility to less sensitive site
Solar facility begins operation while farmland remains available

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A regional council was considering where to build a new renewable-energy facility. The council hoped to build a solar facility near farmland. The plan immediately created disagreement. Some residents welcomed cleaner energy, while farmers worried about losing productive land. The council arranged an independent study of several possible sites and invited residents to comment on the findings. It eventually selected an area with fewer environmental and agricultural conflicts, even though construction would cost slightly more. The council published maps showing the proposed sites and explained how the studies would compare them. Residents were encouraged to submit questions, and the results were discussed at another public meeting. Once the facility opened, the council published a report explaining why the final location had been chosen.

questions.prompt: If you were a council member during the disagreement, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would want objective evidence and a transparent process so that residents understood the trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Should renewable-energy projects be built even when local residents object?
modelAnswers: Public benefits matter, but objections deserve serious consideration. Authorities should explore alternatives and explain decisions transparently.

questions.prompt: Is a rapid transition to clean energy more important than protecting local landscapes?
modelAnswers: Both goals matter, and careful site selection can reduce unnecessary conflicts between them.

questions.prompt: How can governments build public trust in difficult policy decisions?
modelAnswers: They should share evidence early, invite meaningful participation, and explain how public feedback influenced the outcome.

title: Checking Fairness in Educational AI
storyLeadIn: A school district was evaluating a new AI system designed to recommend study materials.

panels.description: Teachers see software recommending different lessons to students
Teacher notices some students repeatedly receive easier material
District investigates training data and adjusts system
Students receive broader study options while teachers monitor recommendations

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A school district was evaluating a new AI system designed to recommend study materials. Teachers had begun using an AI tool that suggested exercises based on past answers. Initially, teachers welcomed the extra support. However, one teacher noticed that some students were repeatedly assigned simple exercises even after making progress. She raised the issue with the district, which reviewed the system's data and decision rules. The investigation showed that earlier mistakes were influencing recommendations too strongly. The district changed the settings and required regular teacher reviews. Teachers examined the system's suggestions alongside each student's recent work. They found that the same learners were receiving repetitive tasks instead of new challenges, even when their answers showed improvement. Students then received a wider range of appropriately challenging materials.

questions.prompt: If you were the teacher who discovered this pattern, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would be concerned that the system was limiting students' opportunities rather than helping them improve.

questions.prompt: Should AI systems make important educational decisions without teacher approval?
modelAnswers: No. Teachers should remain responsible for high-stakes decisions, using automated recommendations only as supporting information.

questions.prompt: Could personalized learning technology increase inequality?
modelAnswers: Yes, if it relies on biased data or unequal access, so fairness checks and teacher involvement are essential.

questions.prompt: What skills will remain important even as AI becomes more capable?
modelAnswers: Critical thinking, creativity, communication, and ethical judgment will remain central to learning and work.

title: A Community Food Cooperative
storyLeadIn: A social entrepreneur was looking for ways to help families struggling with rising food prices.

panels.description: Families compare expensive groceries and leave some items behind
Entrepreneur proposes a member-run food cooperative
Volunteers partner with farmers and arrange bulk purchases
Cooperative opens and members share affordable food while covering costs

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A social entrepreneur was looking for ways to help families struggling with rising food prices. She proposed creating a food cooperative where members could purchase products in larger quantities directly from local farms. Several volunteers agreed to help organize orders and deliveries. At first, the group struggled to estimate demand and cover storage costs. After adjusting the system, the cooperative opened in a small community space and began offering affordable food. Volunteers created a simple system for members to order vegetables in advance. They also built relationships with farmers, who appreciated having a predictable number of orders each week. The entrepreneur was pleased, but she continued reviewing the finances to ensure that the project could survive without constant donations.

questions.prompt: If you were the entrepreneur facing storage costs, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would want a financially sustainable plan so that the cooperative could continue supporting families over the long term.

questions.prompt: Should governments support social enterprises that address food insecurity?
modelAnswers: Yes, when they demonstrate measurable public benefits and manage resources responsibly.

questions.prompt: Can local food systems help communities become more resilient?
modelAnswers: They can diversify supply chains and strengthen relationships with producers, although they cannot replace all wider distribution networks.

questions.prompt: Is access to nutritious food mainly a personal responsibility?
modelAnswers: Individuals make choices, but income, location, and food prices also shape what options are available.

title: Facial Recognition at a Station
storyLeadIn: A transport authority was considering a camera system to improve security at a busy station.

panels.description: Crowded station suffers repeated thefts and officials propose facial recognition
Privacy group asks authority how images will be stored and used
Authority holds public hearing and limits data collection
Station uses revised security plan with clear notices and independent review

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A transport authority was considering a camera system to improve security at a busy station. A supplier recommended installing a facial-recognition system, claiming that it could identify suspects quickly. The authority initially supported the idea, but a privacy group asked how travelers' images would be stored and whether innocent people might be wrongly identified. Officials held a public hearing and commissioned an independent review. They eventually adopted a narrower security plan with strict limits on data collection and clear public notices. The review examined both potential security benefits and the risk of identifying innocent travelers incorrectly. Officials decided that any system would need independent oversight and a clear procedure for complaints. The authority decided to evaluate the program regularly rather than assuming that new technology automatically improved safety.

questions.prompt: If you were an official listening to the privacy concerns, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would want evidence that the technology was effective and that safeguards could prevent misuse or mistaken identification.

questions.prompt: Should facial-recognition technology be used in public places?
modelAnswers: Only in carefully defined situations with strong oversight, transparency, and meaningful limits on data retention.

questions.prompt: Is personal privacy becoming less important to younger generations?
modelAnswers: I do not think so. Many young people value privacy, although they may not understand every way their data is collected.

questions.prompt: Should public safety always take priority over individual freedoms?
modelAnswers: Not automatically. Restrictions on freedom should be necessary, proportionate, and subject to independent review.

title: Restoring a Historic Theater
storyLeadIn: A local historian was trying to save an old theater that had fallen into disrepair.

panels.description: Old theater has leaking roof and a notice of possible demolition
Historian meets residents and business owners to propose restoration
Volunteers and craftspeople repair building while preserving original details
Theater reopens for community performances and residents gather

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A local historian was trying to save an old theater that had fallen into disrepair. The building's roof was leaking, and repairs were expensive. She believed the building was an important part of the town's cultural history. She organized a meeting and invited residents, business owners, and preservation experts to discuss alternatives. With a combination of donations and public funding, the town began a careful restoration project. After months of work, the theater reopened for community performances. Local craftspeople inspected the wooden seats, windows, and stage before work began. They tried to preserve distinctive details while making sure that the restored building would meet modern safety requirements. The historian was delighted to see young performers using a building that had connected generations of residents.

questions.prompt: If you were the historian at the first meeting, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would hope to persuade people that the theater's cultural value justified a realistic restoration plan.

questions.prompt: Should historic buildings be preserved even when restoration is expensive?
modelAnswers: Important buildings deserve protection, but each project should be evaluated for cultural value, cost, and future use.

questions.prompt: Can cultural heritage contribute to local economic development?
modelAnswers: Yes. Well-managed heritage sites can attract visitors and create jobs while strengthening local identity.

questions.prompt: Should modern architecture imitate traditional local styles?
modelAnswers: Not necessarily. New buildings can respect their surroundings without copying the past exactly.

title: Responding to Extreme Heat
storyLeadIn: A city health officer was preparing a summer plan after record-breaking temperatures.

panels.description: Residents wait for buses in direct sun while an older man feels unwell
Officer proposes shaded shelters and public cooling spaces
Workers install shade and local centers extend daytime hours
Residents use cooling spaces during heatwave and officer reviews hospital visits

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A city health officer was preparing a summer plan after record-breaking temperatures. She noticed that many bus stops offered no shade and that older residents living alone were especially vulnerable. During a planning meeting, she recommended installing shaded shelters and opening public cooling spaces. The city worked with local centers to extend their daytime hours and distributed information about heat risks. When the next heatwave arrived, residents had more places to rest and drink water. Community workers distributed information at libraries and clinics, not only through smartphone alerts. The officer also asked volunteers to check on people living alone during the hottest periods. The officer continued collecting health data to evaluate the effectiveness of the measures.

questions.prompt: If you were the officer planning the response, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would prioritize residents most exposed to heat while developing measures that could be maintained in future summers.

questions.prompt: Should cities invest more in adapting to extreme weather?
modelAnswers: Yes. Adaptation can protect lives, although it must be combined with efforts to reduce the causes of climate change.

questions.prompt: Are air-conditioned public spaces a good solution to extreme heat?
modelAnswers: They provide important short-term protection, but cities should also improve shade, building design, and access to drinking water.

questions.prompt: Who should receive priority during periods of extreme heat?
modelAnswers: People at greater risk, including older residents, outdoor workers, and those without safe cooling options, should receive additional support.

title: Giving Students a Voice
storyLeadIn: A school-board member was preparing to review policies that affected teenagers in the district.

panels.description: Students complain that decisions are made without consulting them
Board member invites student representatives to a meeting
Students present survey results and propose timetable adjustments
Board adopts trial schedule and students monitor feedback

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A school-board member was preparing to review policies that affected teenagers in the district. She decided to invite student representatives to a public meeting. Before attending, the students surveyed their classmates and prepared evidence about commuting times and after-school responsibilities. The board listened to their presentation and agreed to test a revised timetable for one term. Although the change did not solve every problem, students appreciated being included in the process. The students rehearsed their presentation and prepared answers to possible questions. They also acknowledged that changing schedules could create difficulties for teachers, showing that they had considered different perspectives. The board member decided to establish a regular student advisory group.

questions.prompt: If you were the board member listening to the students' evidence, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would recognize that students could make informed contributions when given access to information and a genuine opportunity to speak.

questions.prompt: Should teenagers be given more influence over education policy?
modelAnswers: Yes. Their perspectives are essential, but decisions should also consider teachers, families, and long-term educational goals.

questions.prompt: Should the voting age be lowered further in democratic countries?
modelAnswers: It is worth discussing, especially if civic education is strengthened, though the potential effects vary across political systems.

questions.prompt: How can schools encourage meaningful civic participation?
modelAnswers: They can offer student councils with real responsibilities, teach evidence-based debate, and show how decisions are made.

title: Protecting Platform Workers
storyLeadIn: A labor inspector was investigating complaints from people working through delivery apps.

panels.description: Courier studies phone showing long hours and low pay
Workers meet inspector to explain unpredictable earnings
City and companies discuss minimum standards and insurance
Company introduces clearer payments and safety support while inspector monitors results

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A labor inspector was investigating complaints from people working through delivery apps. Couriers had reported unpredictable earnings and unclear insurance coverage. She arranged a meeting where workers could explain their experiences. Some workers valued flexible schedules, but others worried about accidents and sudden changes to payment rules. The inspector contacted the delivery companies and encouraged discussions about minimum standards and transparent contracts. One company later introduced clearer payment information and additional safety support. The companies were asked to explain how payments were calculated and what support workers received after an accident. These discussions helped identify changes that could improve both safety and transparency. The inspector continued monitoring conditions because she knew that flexibility should not come at the cost of basic protections.

questions.prompt: If you were the inspector after hearing the couriers, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would want regulations that protect workers without eliminating the flexibility many of them value.

questions.prompt: Should app-based workers receive benefits similar to regular employees?
modelAnswers: Where they face comparable risks and dependence, basic protections should apply, although benefit systems may need flexible designs.

questions.prompt: Does the gig economy offer more freedom or insecurity?
modelAnswers: It offers both. Workers gain scheduling options but may experience unstable income and limited protection.

questions.prompt: Who should bear the cost of protecting workers in new industries?
modelAnswers: Companies, workers, and public systems may all contribute, but responsibility should reflect who controls the working conditions.

title: A Smart-City Data Project
storyLeadIn: A city technology officer was proposing sensors to improve traffic management.

panels.description: Officer shows dashboard measuring traffic and pedestrian movement
Resident asks whether cameras could track individual people
Team redesigns system to collect anonymous counts and publish safeguards
City launches limited pilot and evaluates traffic patterns without tracking identities

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A city technology officer was proposing sensors to improve traffic management. She argued that the data could help planners reduce congestion and improve safety. During a public meeting, however, a resident asked whether the equipment could identify individual people. The officer realized that the original explanation had not addressed privacy concerns. Her team redesigned the pilot to collect anonymous counts instead of personal records and published a clear description of the safeguards. During the redesign, the team consulted technical experts about ways to reduce the amount of information stored. It also prepared a public document describing the project in everyday language. The project then began on a limited scale, with an independent review scheduled before any expansion.

questions.prompt: If you were the officer after the resident's question, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would recognize that public trust depends on explaining what data is collected and why it is necessary.

questions.prompt: Should cities collect data about residents to improve public services?
modelAnswers: They may collect limited, necessary data, but should minimize personal information and allow independent oversight.

questions.prompt: Can anonymous data ever create privacy risks?
modelAnswers: Yes. Some datasets can be combined to reveal identities, so anonymization must be tested carefully.

questions.prompt: Should citizens be allowed to reject technologies introduced by local government?
modelAnswers: They should have meaningful opportunities to challenge projects and demand safeguards, especially when essential rights may be affected.

title: Autonomous Delivery on Sidewalks
storyLeadIn: A city official was examining a proposal to use small delivery robots in crowded neighborhoods.

panels.description: Delivery company demonstrates robot carrying groceries on sidewalk
Parent with stroller finds narrow pavement partly blocked by robot
Official organizes safety tests with residents and company
Robot follows revised routes and local officials monitor pedestrian access

narration.prompt: Please narrate the story in the four pictures. Start with the printed opening sentence.
modelAnswers: A city official was examining a proposal to use small delivery robots in crowded neighborhoods. A delivery company wanted to use robots on public sidewalks. The robots promised to reduce the need for short delivery trips by car. During a demonstration, however, a parent pushing a stroller had difficulty passing a robot on a narrow pavement. The official organized safety tests with residents, disability advocates, and the company. They agreed on slower speeds and revised routes that avoided busy or narrow walkways. The company agreed to change the software that controlled routes and to create a way for pedestrians to report problems. Officials made clear that the trial would stop if access was repeatedly blocked. The service began on a limited basis, while the city continued checking whether pedestrian access was being protected.

questions.prompt: If you were the official watching the blocked sidewalk, what would you be thinking?
modelAnswers: I would realize that convenience for customers cannot justify creating obstacles for pedestrians, particularly those with mobility needs.

questions.prompt: Should delivery robots be permitted on public sidewalks?
modelAnswers: They can be useful if routes, speed limits, and safety standards are strictly controlled and enforced.

questions.prompt: Will autonomous systems make urban life more convenient?
modelAnswers: They may improve efficiency, but cities must consider accessibility, employment, reliability, and public safety.

questions.prompt: How should governments respond when innovation develops faster than regulations?
modelAnswers: They should use transparent trials, independent evidence, and adaptable rules rather than either banning everything or allowing unrestricted deployment.
